title: ‘His Weakest Creatures’ Director on Offering Hope to Egyptians With His Feel-Good Crime Comedy, Starring Ahmed Helmy and Hend Sabry
description: Egyptian filmmaker Omar Hilal (“Voy! Voy! Voy!”) unites two of the Arab film world’s most bankable stars in his latest feature, “His Weakest Creatu
body:
Egyptian filmmaker Omar Hilal (“Voy! Voy! Voy!”) unites two of the Arab film world’s most bankable stars in his latest feature, “His Weakest Creatures,” a dark comedic thriller that premiered with a gala screening Friday at the Marrakech Film Festival.

	Starring Egyptian comedian and actor Ahmed Helmy (“Wahed Tany”) and Tunisian screen icon Hend Sabry (“Four Daughters”), the film follows a desperate zoologist (Helmy) at Cairo’s crumbling Giza Zoo who agrees to sell animals to a wealthy buyer, pulling him into a dangerous smuggling operation that could save his family — or destroy everything he has spent his life protecting.
	

	Co-written by the director and his brother Ahmed Hilal, the film is produced by Cairo-based Film Clinic and Dubai-based Front Row Filmed Entertainment — who previously collaborated on the local remake of “Perfect Strangers,” the first Arabic-language Netflix original — along with HWC Productions, Film Square, Arabia Pictures and Block 8, in association with Sinai Studios. Front Row is handling the film’s international sales.

	“His Weakest Creatures” was inspired by the incredible, pulled-from-the-headlines story of a spate of mysterious disappearances that took place at the Giza Zoo between 2005 and 2008, when an estimated 400 animals were stolen.

	As with the director’s previous effort, which represented Egypt in the 2024 Oscar race for best international feature, the film focuses on the travails of everyday Egyptians whose fortunes have steadily eroded, along with their hopes for returning their struggling nation to its former glory.
	

	But as with “Voy! Voy! Voy!,” a black comedy about a security guard who attempts to escape Egypt and his dead-end life by faking blindness, Hilal was determined not to make a downbeat drama — to, as he puts it, “paint those stories with a miserable brush.” Instead, he wanted to find the humor — and hope — in the story of the principled Ahmed and his determined wife Hala (Sabry), who are struggling to hold their precarious middle-class lifestyle together.

	In a country whose corrupt elites operate with impunity, the director says he wanted to tell a story where “the weak man wins,” adding: “We need that in Egypt. Because for years, for decades, people are just going on with their lives, but they’re not really living.

	“I found that in this story of thefts happening with the zoo, this ailing zoo, which was a wonder — it was called ‘the jewel of Africa’ — it was a perfect metaphor for Egypt,” he continues. “This place that was the center of everything in the Middle East. And we’ve lost that position.”

	The film’s title comes from the Egyptian proverb “God instills His secret in His weakest creatures.” Hilal describes the adage as “a way for the Egyptian man to find a way out,” clinging to the hope “that somehow, God’s going to save me.”

	The movie takes place in 2007, several years before successive revolutions, in 2011 and 2013, that briefly upended the status quo but “didn’t help create opportunity for the common Egyptian,” Hilal says. “On the contrary, the disparity between the rich and the poor has become much worse.”

	As a result, many Egyptians today feel oddly nostalgic for that era — what the director describes as “a time where you felt a certain safety in stagnation,” despite the rampant corruption that, he says, was pushing the country toward a boiling point.

	Born and raised in Cairo, Hilal knew he wanted to be a filmmaker since the age of 13. But his path to cinema took a lengthy detour, first as a TV director in Italy and later as an adman in Egypt, where he worked as a creative director for global advertising agency Leo Burnett. In 2022, he finally returned to his childhood dream, saying: “Seven, eight hundred commercials later, I made my first movie.”
	

	Upon its release “Voy! Voy! Voy!” was a box-office hit in Egypt and across the Middle East, later embarking on a festival tour that included stops in Marrakech and Rotterdam. Its global rights were picked up by AGC Studios, and with the movie attracting international recognition, Hilal eventually found himself sitting across a desk from a prospective manager in Hollywood.

	It was in the middle of their conversation that the director suddenly remembered a recent Facebook post he’d seen about the animal thefts in Cairo. “I’d just met the man,” he says. “And I told him, ‘Can you hold on one second? Because I have a very bad memory and I just thought of something.’ And I wrote down: zoo robbers.” Thus, a film was born.

	“His Weakest Creatures” is not only grounded in the bygone era of pre-revolution Egypt, but in the leafy Cairo suburb of Maadi, a neighborhood that Hilal says “is still holding on to its Egyptianness.”

	The director describes it as “the last fort” against the rampant consumerism that has overtaken so much of modern-day Egypt. “People who are from Maadi want to hold onto Maadi. They don’t want anything changed about it,” he says. “And that’s the way that I feel. I would love for the simpler Egypt to come back.”

	It’s a feeling that he wanted to evoke in “His Weakest Creatures,” a movie that’s grounded in “kindness,” he says. “It has to make you comfortable and feel like somebody’s giving you a hug.”

	The Marrakech Film Festival runs Nov. 20 – 28.

title: ‘Clarissa’ Directing Duo on How Sophie Okonedo and Star-Studded Ensemble Brought Neon’s Lagos-Set ‘Mrs. Dalloway’ Adaptation to Life
description: It’s been a whirlwind year for Chuko and Arie Esiri, the breakout Nigerian directing duo whose star-studded, Lagos-set “Mrs. Dalloway” reinterpreta
body:
It’s been a whirlwind year for Chuko and Arie Esiri, the breakout Nigerian directing duo whose star-studded, Lagos-set “Mrs. Dalloway” reinterpretation “Clarissa” wowed audiences at this year’s Cannes Film Festival.

	After premiering in the Directors’ Fortnight section of the prestigious French fest, the film set off on a lengthy festival run that’s included stops at the Toronto Intl. Film Festival and the New York Film Festival. It arrives this week in Marrakech, where it plays in the Horizons strand, ahead of a U.S. theatrical release by Neon on Dec. 11.
	

	A reimagining of Virginia Woolf’s classic novel, “Clarissa” follows a society woman as she prepares to host a party at her home in Lagos, where she’ll unexpectedly encounter once-intimate friends from her youth. Reviewing the film in Cannes, Variety’s Jessica Kiang heralded the Esiri duo’s “quietly dazzling Nigerian reinterpretation of ‘Mrs. Dalloway,’” praising “a superb Sophie Okonedo, radiant with melancholy, at the heart of its remarkably well-cast ensemble,” which includes David Oyelowo (“Selma”), India Amarteifio (“Queen Charlotte”), Ayo Edebiri (“The Bear”) and Toheeb Jimoh (“Ted Lasso,” “Industry”).

	“Expanding in ambition and feeling from their promising debut ‘This Is My Desire’ (aka ‘Eyimofe’),” wrote Kiang, “the Esiris cast a perceptive eye over the elite social constellation that has fallen into orbit around this dutiful but unfulfilled society wife, and have nothing but compassion for her as she spins slowly around and around at its center: loved by some, resented by others, admired by all — and totally alone.”
	

	The Esiri Brothers spoke with Variety in Marrakech a day after the film’s well-received regional premiere. Over Moroccan mint tea at the Es Saadi Palace, Chuko described his life-long love affair with Woolf’s groundbreaking novel, which depicts a single day in the life of a society woman in 1920s London.

	It was a book he revisited several years ago, he explained, during a particularly turbulent period for the brothers. “We had made a first feature, it had had a handful of rejections from festivals, Nigeria had had a really bad election,” he said, “and I was thinking a lot about choices, and where we were.

	“I think all of that was swimming within me. So I started looking at it and reading it and feeling the weight of the decisions we make, and how it’s just a collection of small decisions that lead to, like, ‘Fuck, is this it?’” He laughed. “It’s just a series of small things. It’s stunning. It’s staggering how that could happen.”



	

					David Oyelowo and Sophie Okonedo in “Clarissa”
									Courtesy of Neon, Cannes Film Festival
	



	On the surface, transposing a story set in post-WWI London to modern-day Lagos might seem like an unlikely fit, though the directors noted that many of the cultural norms of Nigerian high society were directly imported from the country’s former colonial rulers. 

	“[Clarissa] is a very complicated person that’s hemmed in by tradition and society, and what the British idea of being civilized is,” said Chuko. “But at the same time, there’s this free person — this person that desires more than what she has, or believes that there’s more to life than everything that’s presented to her.” Arie added: “I think that translates to every culture, to every society.”

	“Mrs. Dalloway” masterfully depicted the richly imagined interior lives of her characters, a fact that doesn’t easily lend itself to adaptation for the big screen. Arie praised his brother for “extracting the drama in the book and divorcing himself…from the interior monologues of the characters, whittling it down to the essence of their being, or their presence within this day.” Chuko said his choices largely came down to “putting a lot of faith and trust in the audience,” adding, “and then, obviously, wonderful actors that could bring it out.”
	

	Chief among them is Okonedo, who dazzles in the lead role. During an audience Q&A after the film’s Marrakech screening, Arie recalled a conversation he had with the “Hotel Rwanda” actress once production was underway. “This is such an interior piece of work. How on earth are we going to externalize what’s happening within?” he asked her. Okonedo replied: “If I feel it, you will see it.”

	The brothers also credited Oscar-nominated casting director Nina Gold (“Game of Thrones”), who most recently led the search for the next James Bond, for piecing together “Clarissa’s” star-studded ensemble.

	“That foundation was really laid by Nina Gold,” said Arie. “She talked about casting for essence. She wasn’t so concerned about matching people’s physical attributes as opposed to their essence. That really set us up for success.”

	It certainly didn’t hurt to have a deep pool of acting talent to lean on, with Chuko noting that “it’s always been a dream for us to be a bridge between Nigeria and the diaspora.” Both the U.K.-born Okonedo and the American actress Edebiri trace their paternal roots to Nigeria; Oyelowo and Jimoh’s parents were both born in the West African nation, while Amarteifio is partly of Ghanaian descent.

	During the Marrakech Q&A, Chuko described how the brothers are “trying to expand the canvas of how Lagos and how Nigeria seem,” saying: “I feel there’s an expectation of what films from Africa should look like or feel like, and we wanted to go against that.”

	They’re certainly not alone, with Nigerian filmmakers like Cannes breakout Akinola Davies Jr. (“My Father’s Shadow”) and Sundance prizewinner C.J. Obasi (“Mami Wata”) cementing the country’s cinematic reputation on the world stage.

	For the Esiri Brothers, though, that rising generation of directors is just the foundation for where the industry must go from here.

	“I would really love it to spread beyond writers and directors and into artisans, the same way you had with Cha Cha Cha Films and [Alejandro González] Iñárritu and [Alfonso] Cuarón and [Guillermo] del Toro and the artisans they worked with,” said Chuko. “The DPs, the production designers. I think that’s the next step, to be able to have a pool of really great below-the-line talent that really will unlock it.
	

	“It’s a thing that we’ll see more of, in terms of Nigerian filmmakers playing at large festivals, and Nigerian films being programmed,” he continued. “The train is on that track. It’s now just a question of how you get beyond that space where it feels like it’s a small troupe of arthouse filmmakers. How do you make that more than just a small group of individuals?”

	“We need people to be interested in all aspects of the industry and hone their craft in all sorts of places and come back and make stuff,” added Arie. “Come back and work with us and collaborate.”

	The Marrakech Film Festival runs Nov. 20 – 28.

title: Scout Willis, Will Peltz and Kurt Deimer to Star in Indie Thriller ‘The Prostitute’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Scout Willis, Will Peltz and Kurt Deimer lead the cast of writer-director Paul Boyd’s dark psychological thriller “The Prostitute.”

	The indie fil
body:
Scout Willis, Will Peltz and Kurt Deimer lead the cast of writer-director Paul Boyd’s dark psychological thriller “The Prostitute.”

	The indie film stars Peltz (“Euphoria,” “Manifest,” “Unfriended”) as a young, struggling filmmaker living out of his van in Hollywood who becomes fixated on documenting a mysterious blonde woman (Willis) he encounters on the streets. As he immerses himself in her world in pursuit of the story that will make his career, he finds himself drawn into a dangerous web of secrets, violence and obsession that blurs the line between observer and participant.
	

	Principal photography is underway, and the film will shoot entirely in Los Angeles. Eric Barrett is producing for Mirror Films, and Deimer (“Halloween 2018,” “Scared to Death,” “Hellbilly Hollow,” “Trading Paint”) is executive producing through his Bald Man Films banner.

	Blending found-footage intimacy with narrative intensity, “The Prostitute” explores the dark intersection of content creation, voyeurism and true-crime obsession in modern Los Angeles. 

	“This is a raw, unsettling story about the cost of chasing a story,” Boyd (“Scared to Death,” “Vicious Circle”) said in a statement. “We’re thrilled to have this cast in front of the camera, exploring the thin line between art and exploitation on the streets of Los Angeles.”

	Barrett added, “Paul has written a provocative and timely thriller that feels both intimate and explosive. Pairing him with this cast and Kurt’s genre expertise through Bald Man Films creates the perfect team to bring ‘The Prostitute’ to the screen.”
	

	Peltz is represented by Thruline Entertainment and Buchwald. Deimer is represented by Jade Waechter, Bald Man, LLC, DRPR, High Roads Collective and Regime Music Group. Willis is represented by Alex Cole of Elevate Entertainment, Hard Launch Partner Group, WME, Atlantic (10K Projects), Warner Chappell, 42West and CCGG, LLP.

title: Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival Opens With Lawrence Fajardo’s ‘Silenced Nights’ and a Call to Face Reality
description: The 21st Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF) kicked off Nov. 28 at the Empire XXI cinema in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, with Filipino director Lawre
body:
The 21st Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF) kicked off Nov. 28 at the Empire XXI cinema in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, with Filipino director Lawrence Fajardo’s thriller “Silenced Nights” as its opening film. 

	The evening’s gentle drizzle stopped shortly after the ceremony began.

	Festival founder Garin Nugroho introduced this edition’s theme, “Influx,” which casts filmmakers in the ecosystem as surfers. “Together – you, us, and the guests – we are able to surf to keep cinema alive throughout this country,” Nugroho said.
	

	The ceremony then took a political turn. Festival president Ifa Isfansyah and festival director Budi Irawanto invited the audience to reflect on the unsettling state of the world, pointing to natural and political crises and social inequality that threaten people’s safety.

	“A festival must not be a space separate from reality; it cannot just be a place to escape from problems out there. Instead, a festival must be a space to face reality, open up conversations, bring together various perspectives, and preserve the possibility of critical thinking,” said Irawanto, who then asked attendees to stand for a moment of silence.

	Fajardo thanked the festival and said the film is personally meaningful to him. “Silenced Nights,” set against extrajudicial killings in a Philippine urban community, played in the Platform competition at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.

	Indonesian singer Mondo Gascaro closed the night with a live set that opened with the soothing “Butiran Angin” and took in “Senandung Lagu Lama,” from Usmar Ismail’s 1956 musical “Tiga Dara” (“Three Maidens”); “Apatis,” composed for Nugroho’s “Kucumbu Tubuh Indahku” (“Memories of My Body”); and “Dan Bila.”
	

	The main competition includes two Cannes titles: Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown,” which won the Fipresci prize in Critics’ Week, and Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s Directors’ Fortnight selection “9 Temples to Heaven.” Also competing are Indonesian director Jeremias Nyangoen’s “Black Coffee” and Japanese animation “Cherry and Virgin.” A slate of non-screening events is open to the public.

	JAFF Market, the industry arm of the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival, runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta. The festival’s 21st edition runs through Dec. 5.

title: Migrant Worker Tale ‘Luz and Flor’ Finds Prehistoric Filipino and Indonesian Humans in Spain at JAFF Market
description: Two prehistoric humans, one from the Philippines and one from Indonesia, cross paths as laborers in Spain in “Luz and Flor,” the new feature projec
body:
Two prehistoric humans, one from the Philippines and one from Indonesia, cross paths as laborers in Spain in “Luz and Flor,” the new feature project from Filipino filmmaker Glenn Barit (“Cleaners”). The project, also known as “Luzonensis and Floresiensis,” is among the 2026 JAFF Future Project selections at JAFF Market.

	With Spain’s property market collapsing around them, the pair look for a place to belong and a way to get by, while the echoes of colonial rule go unresolved.
	

	The project was recently selected for the International Film Festival Rotterdam’s CineMart 2027 and won the Talents Tokyo Award in 2025. It took part in the QCinema Project Market in Quezon City, Philippines, in 2025, and has been through the West Meets East Screenplay Lab 2026 in Dhaka, the Film Development Council of the Philippines’ Isapelikula Script Lab in Manila and the AFANxPaS Young Filmmakers Bootcamp 2026, held in Manila, Bangkok and Paris.

	“When I was young, I used to frequent the caves where the bones of the Homo luzonensis were discovered. It is known to be the earliest ancient human species in the Philippines,” Barit says. “So I became curious about this caveman character and the history that he might carry and represent.”

	A 2023 trip to Jogja, as Yogyakarta is known, left Barit struck by how alike Filipinos and Indonesians are, and how different. “I feel like we are two nations blurred by modern ideas of nations and borders,” he says. Homo luzonensis is also thought to be a close relative of Homo floresiensis, a species found on Indonesia’s Flores Island.

	Barit wanted to drop the two characters into present-day struggles, as migrants in countries that once ruled their own. “I’m curious about these intersections as well as their ironies. How these supposedly ‘primitive’ figures might have something to say about our modern world,” he says. “It also just seems exciting to research about and a bit funny to shoot.”
	

	He is aiming for a tone that is thoughtful but playful. “Maybe a way of interrogating serious and tough questions through something absurd and imaginative,” Barit says.

	The film is produced by Kristine De Leon of the Philippines and Tanveer Hossain of Bangladesh through their company Katalog. The feature grows out of Barit’s short “Luzonensis Osteoporosis,” which played festivals abroad.

	“Glenn Barit has an extraordinary ability to tell stories that feel fresh, inventive, and distinctly his own, without ever chasing trends,” De Leon says. “Tanveer Hossain and I were immediately drawn to the short film. We found it beautifully crafted, thoughtfully directed, and full of creative possibilities.”

	The pair worked together for several years before setting up Katalog. “As producers from the Philippines and Bangladesh, we believe in bringing filmmakers and creative voices from different countries together through meaningful co-productions,” De Leon says. “‘Luz and Flor’ is a wonderful example of this vision.”

	The screenplay is in its second draft, with the next draft underway, and the team is preparing for more research, notably in Spain, along with further creative consultations. Financing is planned for next year. At JAFF Market, the producers hope to bring Indonesian talent on board – a co-producer, a writing partner and a performer – to give the story’s Indonesian side authenticity. They are also courting funders, sales agents and festival programmers.

	Barit, meanwhile, is preparing a short backed by the Film Development Council of the Philippines that he will shoot 50 times, each time with a different cast, and is in early development on a romance feature about pet custody.

	JAFF Market, the industry arm of the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival, runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta. The festival’s 21st edition runs Nov. 28–Dec. 5.

title: A Demon Baby and a Contract-Killing Company Anchor Indonesian Dark Comedy ‘Gokill’ at JAFF Market
description: Selected for the 2026 JAFF Future Project, supernatural dark comedy “Gokill” follows Sugeng and Ratna, a married couple who finally conceive a chil
body:
Selected for the 2026 JAFF Future Project, supernatural dark comedy “Gokill” follows Sugeng and Ratna, a married couple who finally conceive a child after years of trying.

	Their joy turns to desperation when doctors discover that their unborn child is unlikely to survive. The couple turns to black magic, binding Sugeng to Silly, a demon baby that feeds on human organs. To save their unborn child, they must help Silly grow into adulthood.
	

	As Sugeng struggles to keep up with the demon baby’s appetite, he discovers that the cleaning company he works for, Gokill, harbors a dark secret: it also operates a contract-killing division.

	Writer-director Amanda Iswan made her directorial debut with “Zeta: When the Dead Awaken” (2019). “I’ve always been fascinated by how easily love can become the perfect excuse for doing terrible things,” Iswan says. “What I find interesting about dark comedy is that we can find ourselves laughing at situations we would normally find disturbing, or sympathizing with characters whose actions we would normally condemn.”

	A short film of the same title, also written, directed and produced by Iswan, screened at the 2025 Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival. The feature project, however, develops a distinct premise centered on the demon baby and Gokill’s hidden operations.

	“What excites me about ‘Gokill’ is how it takes this very real economic anxiety and explores it through an absurd supernatural premise,” producers James Erlangga, Damar Ardi and Aufa Ariaputra tell Variety. “Despite its fantastical elements, Sugeng’s struggles are something many people experience in their everyday lives.”
	

	“Gokill” previously received the Pitching Forum MTN Development Grant and the BSM Premiere Gear Fund at Jakarta Film Week 2026.

	The project is currently in development under Angin Segar Films, Kapsul Waktu Studio and Satu Atap, with Iswan refining the screenplay and shaping the film’s creative and visual direction.

	“Our main goal at JAFF Market is to secure funding and find the right partners to move ‘Gokill’ from development toward production,” the producers say. “Beyond financing, we’re also interested in exploring the film’s potential in the international market. We believe ‘Gokill’ has a distinctive premise and universal themes that can resonate with audiences beyond Indonesia.”

	JAFF Market, the industry arm of the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival, runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta. The festival’s 21st edition runs Nov. 28–Dec. 5.

title: Planning a Holiday Trip to New York City? These Hilton Hotels Put You Steps From the City’s Most Festive Attractions
description:
Nov 28, 2026 6:00am PT	
	


		Planning a Holiday Trip to New York City? These Hilton Hotels Put You Steps From the City’s Most Festi
body:
Nov 28, 2026 6:00am PT	
	


		Planning a Holiday Trip to New York City? These Hilton Hotels Put You Steps From the City’s Most Festive Attractions
	
	
			


			
			
	

	

		
	
				
	If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	There’s New York, and then there’s New York at Christmas.

	Few cities have played a more memorable role in holiday movies, from Kevin McCallister’s extravagant Manhattan adventure in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York” to Buddy the Elf’s wide-eyed arrival in “Elf.” And every December, the city does a pretty convincing job of living up to its Hollywood reputation. Fifth Avenue storefronts become elaborate holiday displays, Rockefeller Center unveils its towering Christmas tree and Bryant Park transforms into a winter village complete with ice skating, holiday shopping and hot chocolate.
	

	Of course, the real-life version also comes with crowded sidewalks, sold-out Broadway shows and some of the most expensive hotel rooms of the year. Choosing the right place to stay can make all the difference, particularly when many of the season’s biggest attractions are within walking distance.

	For a holiday stay in New York City, Hilton offers several Midtown options near major seasonal attractions: The Draper New York, Tapestry Collection by Hilton, walking distance from Bryant Park’s Winter Village, New York Hilton Midtown near Rockefeller Center and Radio City Music Hall, and Tempo by Hilton New York Times Square for travelers who want to stay directly in Times Square.

	But make sure to book your stay directly Hilton’s website or Hilton Honors app, where travelers can access its Price Match Guarantee. Meanwhile, Hilton Honors members can take advantage of exclusive rates and earn points toward future stays. The free loyalty program also offers digital check-in, room selection and Digital Key access, allowing guests to skip the front desk and head straight to their room.
	

	Best of all, Hilton Honors Members save 20% when they book by December 22, for eligible stays through April 2, 2027. And with the More Points to Play offer, you can earn up to 3,000 Bonus Points on stays through December 31. Book now on Hilton.com or the Hilton Honors app. Terms apply.

		

	

	
					
		

					The Draper New York, Tapestry Collection by Hilton		

	
		For families who prefer a little breathing room between holiday festivities, The Draper New York offers a stylish home base just far enough from the Times Square crowds. Tucked off Fifth Avenue on West 37th Street, the 143-room boutique hotel puts guests within walking distance of Bryant Park’s Winter Village, Macy’s famous holiday window displays and the Empire State Building.Part of Hilton’s Tapestry Collection, the 23-story property combines contemporary interiors with a more intimate atmosphere than Midtown’s sprawling hotels. Connecting rooms (subject to availability) allow families to stay close while giving everyone their own space to recharge after a day of sightseeing, while select accommodations feature private furnished balconies with sweeping city views.Whether the day’s plans call for an early morning of ice skating, an afternoon of Fifth Avenue shopping or an evening Broadway show, the hotel’s central location makes it easy for families to explore at their own pace — and return for a midday break when little legs need a rest.	
		
	

		

	

	
					
		

					New York Hilton Midtwon		

	
		If your ideal New York Christmas itinerary involves Rockefeller Center’s famous tree, Radio City Music Hall’s Christmas Spectacular and a shopping trip along Fifth Avenue, it’s hard to beat the location of New York Hilton Midtown. The sprawling hotel sits on Sixth Avenue between West 53rd and 54th streets, directly across from the Museum of Modern Art and just two blocks from Rockefeller Center. Central Park, St. Patrick’s Cathedral and the luxury storefronts lining Fifth Avenue are also within easy walking distance.Rooms feature Hilton Serenity beds, work desks and skyline views, while select higher-floor accommodations offer glimpses of Central Park. Guests booking executive-level suites can also take advantage of the hotel’s Executive Lounge. But the hotel is also well-suited for families and larger groups, with a wide selection of guest rooms, connecting accommodations and spacious one- and two-bedroom suites.For families traveling together, connecting rooms and spacious one- and two-bedroom suites offer room to spread out without sacrificing time together — particularly welcome after a long day of sightseeing, holiday shopping and Broadway shows. Dining options are just as flexible, whether it’s a quick breakfast or grab-and-go snacks at Herb N’ Kitchen before heading out to see the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree, or cocktails and light bites at the Lobby Lounge after an evening in the city. With everything under one roof, guests can make the most of their holiday itinerary without having to plan every moment around it.Ahead of Thanksgiving, the property has another major selling point: its location directly on the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade route. Hilton offers specially designated parade-view rooms and suites overlooking Sixth Avenue, allowing guests to watch the balloons pass from the comfort of their accommodations. The hotel also hosts a Thanksgiving buffet at Herb N’ Kitchen, featuring more than 20 dishes and over 10 desserts. However, designated parade-view rooms require multi-night stays and carry premium rates, so booking early is particularly important.	
		
	

		

	

	
					
		

					Tempo by Hilton New York Times Square		

	
		For travelers who prefer their New York holidays with a little more Broadway, Tempo by Hilton New York Times Square offers a front-row seat to the action. Opened in 2023 as the first property from Hilton’s Tempo lifestyle brand, the 661-room hotel occupies 36 floors of the 46-story TSX Broadway development, which also houses the historic Palace Theatre. Its address, 1568 Broadway, puts guests directly in Times Square, with Rockefeller Center, Bryant Park and Radio City Music Hall all within walking distance.Guest rooms are designed around three distinct areas: a dedicated “Get Ready Zone” for working, dining or preparing for a night out; a spacious bathroom with an oversized shower, Bluetooth speaker mirror and Apotheke bath products; and a sleeping area equipped with cooling linens, Sealy mattresses and a 65-inch television. Floor-to-ceiling windows offer city views, while lighting automatically adjusts throughout the day. The hotel also has nine specialty Wellness Rooms outfitted with Peloton bikes, yoga mats and resistance bands, plus a 24-hour fitness center.One of the property’s biggest draws is Highball, its 11th-floor restaurant and cocktail lounge, which opens onto an expansive outdoor terrace overlooking Times Square. The menu includes everything from truffle Parmesan fries and house-made meatballs to burgers and flatbreads, along with inventive cocktails and nonalcoholic alternatives. Downstairs, the hotel’s cafe serves coffee, breakfast options and lighter grab-and-go fare.Broadway fans have another reason to book this season. In September, Tempo unveiled a themed suite inspired by the Tony-winning musical “The Lost Boys, “available for stays through Sept. 14, 2027. The room recreates the show’s fictional California boardwalk town with a glowing Ferris wheel mural, vintage television and VCR, vinyl records and other 1980s-inspired details. Guests booking the specialty suite also receive themed merchandise, a welcome treat and a food-and-beverage credit, while Highball is offering a corresponding cocktail and prix fixe menu.For travelers who want to experience the Times Square countdown from the comfort of their room, the hotel offers select Ball Drop room categories with views of the Times Square New Year’s Eve celebration. Among them is the Presidential Suite, which features a separate living area, dining room and kitchenette. The views are specific to these room categories, making advance booking essential for travelers hoping to watch the countdown from upstairs.

title: Indonesian Social Thriller ‘A Quiet Sunshine’ Speaks Up for Women’s Bodily Autonomy at JAFF Market
description: Indonesian writer-director Ninndi Raras’ debut project “A Quiet Sunshine” is among the projects selected for the 2026 JAFF Future Project at JAFF M
body:
Indonesian writer-director Ninndi Raras’ debut project “A Quiet Sunshine” is among the projects selected for the 2026 JAFF Future Project at JAFF Market.

	The story follows the intuitive bond between two women living on a remote Indonesian island: Melyana, a midwife, and Amira, a 17-year-old who became pregnant as a result of a sexual assault. Facing a fleeting 14-week legal abortion window and an unsupportive social system, they decide to escape the island in search of freedom.
	

	“I want to show a quiet act of resistance. Melyana and Amira aren’t trying to change the world. They simply break the rules to build a safe space and reclaim their own bodies. I hope the audience walks away feeling the power of that quiet solidarity,” Raras tells Variety.

	The project stems from Raras’ own experience of sexual assault as a teenager. Years later, she went through pregnancy herself.

	“If a consensual pregnancy already demands so much, what happens when a woman is forced to carry a child without consent? Her own body becomes an uninvited collaborator,” she says.

	Raras, the mother of a daughter, is concerned that systemic inequality that can strip women of autonomy is deeply embedded around the world. “I want [my daughter] to grow up in a world where she is never a victim of this system, and where she always owns her body,” the director says.

	Giovanni Rahmadeva of QUN Films boarded the project as a producer because “it captures that exact clash between society’s loud, suffocating outrage and the quiet, unshakeable calm of women reclaiming their own bodies.” Rahmadeva values the role of midwives as a symbol of women caring for and protecting one another under male-dominated power.
	

	“Sharing women’s real stories isn’t just a gesture; it’s the core of our creative mission. Based on true events, this story brings forward truths that are often silenced by strict traditions,” says Rahmadeva.

	Backed by QUN Films and Catchlight Pictures, the project is at the advanced script stage and aims to move into pre-production and shooting by mid-2027. At JAFF Market, the team is looking to meet international co-producers, sales agents and distributors to close the financing gap.

	JAFF Market, the industry arm of the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival, runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta. The festival’s 21st edition runs Nov. 28–Dec. 5.

title: ‘Beauty and the Beast’ Becomes a Tale of Coercive Control in Romantic Thriller ‘Wreck and Ruin’ at JAFF Market
description:
Australian director Rosie Lourde’s debut project “Wreck and Ruin” is being presented at the 2026 JAFF Future Project at JAFF Market.

	Set in 1893
body:
Australian director Rosie Lourde’s debut project “Wreck and Ruin” is being presented at the 2026 JAFF Future Project at JAFF Market.

	Set in 1893 on a tropical volcanic island with black-sand coastlines, the story follows Elizabeth, who has just lost her sister Christina in a shipwreck, as she falls in love with Louis. As Christina’s vision appears, Elizabeth realizes Louis is hiding a terrifying secret that could threaten her life.


	Written by Katharine McPhee, who is also a producer on the project, the script turns the classic story of love as salvation on its head and asks: what happens when the lover doesn’t want to be saved, but only wants to possess the other?
	

	“I was drawn to the visceral tension of Katharine taking the classic fairy tale of ‘Beauty and the Beast‘ and flipping it into a survival thriller about coercive control,” Lourde tells Variety. “Setting that psychological trap against little-known Australian maritime history across the Indonesian archipelago felt electric, visually stunning and timely.”

	The $2.5 million project is in advanced development with a polished draft of the script, and is designed to combine on-location production in Indonesia with Australian grants and post-production. Cinematographer Nicola Daley (“The Handmaid’s Tale”) and award-winning composer Caitlin Yeo (“The Butterfly Tree,” “The Rocket”) are on board.

	“I want audiences, especially young women watching together, to experience a heart-pounding gothic ‘romantasy’ thrill ride that celebrates female solidarity and reminds them that real love never traps you; it sets you free,” says the director.
	

	For McPhee, the script is a passion project she has been personally committed to for several years. “I believe in its strong commercial appeal as a genre film, as well as its timely story and themes,” McPhee tells Variety. “The attachment of Rosie as director and producer has bolstered the project. I’m so excited to see it continue to evolve as an enticing project in today’s marketplace.”

	At JAFF Market, the team hopes to connect with equity financiers, regional buyers and key production partners.

	Alongside “Wreck and Ruin,” Lourde is executive producing Nick Annas’ “Crashout,” which will world premiere at an A-list U.S. festival in early 2027. She is also developing her queer psychosexual thriller “Blackout” and is in post-production on the feature documentary “The Long Game,” which she is directing, about Chinese-Australian football history in the 1800s.

	JAFF Market, the industry arm of the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival, runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta. The festival’s 21st edition runs Nov. 28–Dec. 6.

title: Rishab Shetty Wins Best Actor for ‘Kantara: A Legend – Chapter 1′ as Tiago Guedes’ ‘Aqui’ Takes Golden Peacock at International Film Festival of India
description: Portuguese filmmaker Tiago Guedes’ Spanish-language film “Aqui” won the Golden Peacock for Best Film at the 57th International Film Festival of Ind
body:
Portuguese filmmaker Tiago Guedes’ Spanish-language film “Aqui” won the Golden Peacock for Best Film at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), which concluded in Goa on Nov. 28. 

	Produced by Paulo Branco, “Aqui” received the festival’s top award, with the jury praising its ability to transport audiences into “a comforting and dreamlike universe that, despite its unpredictability, feels like one we belong to and don’t wish to leave.” The director and producer share the award and its INR5.1 million ($57,000) cash prize.
	

	Kannada cinema actor-director Rishab Shetty won the Silver Peacock for Best Actor (Male) for “Kantara: A Legend – Chapter 1,” which also received a Special Mention. German filmmaker Volker Schlöndorff was named Best Director for “Visitation,” while Maya O’Rourke won Best Actor (Female) for “The Meltdown.”

	The Silver Peacock for Best Debut Feature Film of a Director was awarded to Bérenger Thouin for “The Golden Age.” The jury commended the director’s vision in blending archival material with real footage to create an ambitious and compelling period film. Thouin’s brother Céleste, the film’s composer, accepted the award on the director’s behalf.

	The Silver Peacock for Special Jury Award went to Argentine film “The River Train,” directed by Lorenzo Ferro and Lucas A. Vignale. The ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal, which recognizes a film reflecting the ideals promoted by UNESCO and the values associated with Mahatma Gandhi, was awarded to “Rahma,” directed by Turkish filmmaker Faysal Soysal.

	Vishal Chaturvedi’s “Hanuman Ansh” won Best Debut Director of an Indian Feature Film. The jury praised the film for bringing together culture, faith and music with a strong emotional connection. The Best Web Series (OTT) award went to “Made in India: A Titan Story,” directed by Robbie Grewal. Its citation praised the story of “dreams realized and aspirations fulfilled across India.”
	

	The closing ceremony, held at the Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Indoor Stadium, featured music and dance performances. Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting secretary Chanchal Kumar, festival director Ashutosh Gowariker and international jury chair Aanand L. Rai were among those present. Sawant also honored award-winning Goan filmmaker Aditya Suhas Jambhale.

	“When we speak about film festivals, we are really celebrating two simple things: the stories and strangers who turn into friends,” Sawant said in his address.

	Gowariker, reflecting on his first year as festival director, said his aim had been to push IFFI forward rather than repeat what had been done before. He acknowledged that the festival had not gotten everything right, said those experiences would serve as lessons, and thanked filmmakers and the people of Goa. “We laugh and cry together, and we feel the pain of someone miles away,” he said.

	Kumar spoke about IFFI’s place in the history of Indian cinema and its role in bringing Indian and international films together. “May the great next story that catches the world begin its journey from India,” he said.

	This edition screened more than 150 international films from 86 countries, with Spain as Country of Honor and Russia as Partner Country, alongside a BRICS showcase.

	The full list of winners:

	Golden Peacock, Best Film “Aqui,” dir. Tiago Guedes, prod. Paulo Branco

	Best Director Volker Schlöndorff, “Visitation”

	Best Actor (Male) Rishab Shetty, “Kantara: A Legend Chapter 1”

	Best Actor (Female) Maya O’Rourke, “The Meltdown”

	Special Jury Award “The River Train,” dir. Lorenzo Ferro, Lucas A. Vignale

	Best Debut Feature Film of a Director Bérenger Thouin, “The Golden Age”

	Best Debut Director of an Indian Feature Film Vishal Chaturvedi, “Hanuman Ansh”

	Best Web Series (OTT) “Made in India: A Titan Story,” dir. Robbie Grewal

	ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal “Rahma,” dir. Faysal Soysal

	Special Mention“Kantara: A Legend Chapter 1”

title: 'The Challenge' Star Tyler Duckworth Cause of Death Revealed
description:
'The Challenge' Alum Tyler Duckworth
                          Cause of Death Revealed
body:
'The Challenge' Alum Tyler Duckworth
                          Cause of Death Revealed
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              "The Challenge" star Tyler Duckworth died from a heart issue ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
              According to the North Dakota State Forensic Examiner’s Office, Tyler died from hypertensive cardiovascular disease ... and his manner of death was ruled natural.
      
    
              Hypertensive cardiovascular disease is a heart condition caused by elevated blood pressure over years or decades.
      

              As you know, Tyler died in August after being found in an overflowing bathtub. A downstairs neighbor complained of water coming through the ceiling ... and  "tried to get the water shut off" and was "not able to confirm" whether Tyler was alive.
      
    
              We were told there were no outside signs of trauma found on Tyler's body.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              He was honored that same month at his funeral, attended by his co-stars from both "The Real World" and "The Challenge."
      
    
              Tyler made his final public appearance at a "Challenge Mania" event in Minneapolis just weeks before he died. He appeared on "The Challenge" in 2006, and won "Cutthroat" in 2010 and “Rivals” in 2011 before returning for "All Stars 2" in 2021.
      
    
              Tyler was 44 years old.
